Case Study

From Laptop Script to a Secure, Event-Driven AWS Pipeline

Building a banking transaction ingestion system in five phases — starting as a local Go & MongoDB experiment and ending as a serverless, Secrets Manager–backed architecture on AWS, with no hardcoded credentials anywhere in the code.

Richard · Terraform · AWS Lambda (Python) · ECS Fargate (Go) · Amazon S3 · Secrets Manager · MongoDB Atlas

The goal was simple to state and, as usual, less simple to build correctly: ingest a stream of bank transaction events — new accounts, deposits, withdrawals, account closures — and keep a MongoDB collection of accounts and their transaction history accurately in sync. What changed across five phases wasn't the core logic — it was everything around it: where the code ran, where the data lived, and who was allowed to touch either one.

Phase 1 — Local Prototype

Local MongoDB · Local files

Proving the domain logic first

The first version ran entirely on my machine: a local MongoDB instance, and two Go files splitting responsibility cleanly — mongo.go owned the persistence layer (the Account/Transaction schema, the database connection, and the upsert logic), while transactions.go owned ingestion: reading a flat file of comma-separated events line by line and routing each one to create an account, record a transaction, or deactivate an account. No cloud services yet — the point of Phase 1 was getting the data model and the update logic right before worrying about where any of it would eventually run.

Phase 2 — Migrating to MongoDB Atlas

Cloud database

Swapping local Mongo for a managed cluster

Once the ingestion logic worked locally, the local MongoDB instance was retired in favor of MongoDB Atlas — a managed, cloud-hosted cluster reachable from outside my laptop. Functionally this was a small change: a mongodb://localhost:27017 connection string became an Atlas mongodb+srv:// URI, and the driver was pinned to a specific Server API version (options.ServerAPI) as Atlas recommends for compatibility. Same structs, same upsert logic — but now the data lived somewhere durable, which is what made every later phase possible.

Phase 3 — Dockerizing the Go Service

Containerization

Making the service portable

Next, the Go program was packaged into a Docker image so it could run consistently anywhere — a compiled Go binary in a minimal container, still reading its input file from a local path and writing to Atlas. On the surface this looks like a small step (go run transactions.go became docker run), but it's the step that made Phase 4 possible: a container image is portable in a way a binary tied to my machine's filesystem simply isn't.

Phase 4 — Moving to AWS

S3 · ECR · Fargate · Lambda

From "docker run" to an event-driven pipeline

This is where the architecture became genuinely distributed, in three moves. The input file moved from a local path to Amazon S3 — files land in a bucket instead of a folder. The Docker image moved from a local daemon to Amazon ECR, so AWS could pull and run it. And instead of a person running docker run, the container now launches as an AWS Fargate task — a serverless container with no EC2 instance to patch or manage.

Tying it together: an S3 ObjectCreated event notification fires a Lambda function the moment a file lands in the bucket. The Lambda's entire job is to resolve the account's default VPC networking (subnets, security group) and call ecs:RunTask, passing only the bucket name and file key as overrides — the two values that are genuinely different on every invocation:

# lambda_payload.py — trigger the Fargate task
response = ecs_client.run_task(
    cluster='fargate-cluster',
    taskDefinition='first_national_bank',
    launchType='FARGATE',
    networkConfiguration={
        'awsvpcConfiguration': {
            'subnets': subnet_ids,
            'securityGroups': [security_group_id],
            'assignPublicIp': 'ENABLED'
        }
    },
    overrides={
        'containerOverrides': [{
            'name': 'first_national_bank',
            'environment': [
                {'name': 'BUCKET_NAME', 'value': bucket_name},
                {'name': 'FILE_KEY', 'value': file_key}
            ]
        }]
    }
)

Nothing runs unless a file actually shows up — the pipeline went from something I kicked off by hand to a properly event-driven system.

Phase 5 — Closing the Loop on Secrets

Security hardening

No more hardcoded credentials

The last piece closed a gap that's extremely common in early-stage projects: the MongoDB Atlas connection string — username, password, and all — was sitting directly in the Lambda's source code, passed to the Fargate task as a plaintext environment variable on every invocation. During a security pass, that came out entirely. The credentials moved into AWS Secrets Manager as a single JSON secret; the ECS task definition now resolves four individual fields (username, password, host, app_name) straight out of that secret, and only the ECS execution role — never the running application, never the Lambda — is permitted to read it:

// main.tf — the secret and least-privilege read access
resource "aws_secretsmanager_secret" "mongo_credentials" {
  name        = "first_national_bank/mongo_credentials"
  description = "MongoDB Atlas connection details"
}

resource "aws_iam_role_policy" "ecs_secrets_access" {
  role = aws_iam_role.ecs_execution_role.id
  policy = jsonencode({
    Statement = [{
      Effect   = "Allow"
      Action   = ["secretsmanager:GetSecretValue"]
      Resource = aws_secretsmanager_secret.mongo_credentials.arn
    }]
  })
}

On the Go side, the service no longer expects one pre-built MONGO_URI — it reassembles the connection string from four environment variables that ECS injects automatically at task launch:

// mongo.go
func buildMongoURI() string {
    username := os.Getenv("MONGO_USERNAME")
    password := os.Getenv("MONGO_PASSWORD")
    host     := os.Getenv("MONGO_HOST")
    appName  := os.Getenv("MONGO_APP_NAME")

    return fmt.Sprintf("mongodb+srv://%s:%s@%s/?appName=%s",
        url.QueryEscape(username), url.QueryEscape(password), host, appName)
}

A debug log line that had been printing the full connection string — password included — to CloudWatch was also removed, and the exposed credential itself was rotated in Atlas the same day it was found. The result: the secret exists in exactly one place, it's injected automatically at container launch, and it never touches source control, logs, or Lambda code again.

Final Stack

Terraform Python Go Amazon S3 AWS Lambda ECS Fargate Amazon ECR Secrets Manager MongoDB Atlas IAM

Lessons Learned & What's Next

A few things a security-focused pass surfaced that are worth naming honestly rather than editing out of the story:

Bucket access

An early Terraform draft granted the S3 bucket public read access for convenience while testing. That's being removed — access should only ever go through the Fargate task's IAM role, which already has exactly the S3 permissions it needs.

Idempotency — fixed

The upsert logic now runs in two steps: first ensure the account document exists, then append the transaction only if that ID isn't already present — with no upsert on the second write. A retried transaction ID is now a safe no-op instead of risking a duplicate account document.

Task vs. service — fixed

The standing aws_ecs_service and its dedicated security group have been removed from the Terraform entirely. Only the event-driven one-shot task that Lambda launches via run_task() remains — nothing runs unless a file actually shows up.

Rotation

Secrets Manager supports automatic rotation via a scheduled Lambda. Manual rotation (see the Operations Runbook below) is fine for now; wiring up automatic rotation is a natural next step.

Remote state

Local Terraform state caused a real incident mid-build — an apply run from a second local directory drifted out of sync with reality and broke a working deployment. Moving to a shared remote backend (S3 + DynamoDB locking) is next, so state can't fork like that again.

Operations Runbook

The commands below cover the day-to-day lifecycle of this project — first-time setup, testing a change, rotating credentials, and tearing it down — collected here as a quick reference rather than scattered across shell history.

1Install

Provision everything — S3, Lambda, ECR, the ECS cluster and task definition, IAM roles, and an empty Secrets Manager secret container:

terraform init
terraform apply

Populate the secret with real credentials — this is a one-time, out-of-band step, never something Terraform manages directly:

aws secretsmanager put-secret-value \
  --secret-id first_national_bank/mongo_credentials \
  --region us-east-1 \
  --secret-string '{"username":"...","password":"...","host":"...","database":"retail_banking","app_name":"Cluster0"}'

Build and push the container image so the task definition has something to pull:

docker build -t first_national_bank .
docker tag first_national_bank <account-id>.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/first_national_bank:latest
docker push <account-id>.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/first_national_bank:latest

2Test

Drop the sample file into the bucket to fire the whole chain — S3 event → Lambda → Fargate task:

aws s3 cp data/<test-file> s3://<bucket-name>/

Bucket name is generated with a random suffix at apply time — find the current one with aws s3 ls | grep transactions-offload. Then watch the ECS cluster's Tasks tab (including Stopped, since this is a one-shot task) and the /ecs/first_national_bank CloudWatch log group. A clean run ends with the file deleted from the bucket automatically.

3Reload / rotate the secret

Update the Mongo credentials at any time — no Terraform change and no redeploy required, since ECS resolves the secret fresh on every new task launch:

aws secretsmanager put-secret-value \
  --secret-id first_national_bank/mongo_credentials \
  --region us-east-1 \
  --secret-string '{"username":"...","password":"<new password>","host":"...","database":"retail_banking","app_name":"Cluster0"}'

4Forcibly remove the secret

Secrets Manager soft-deletes by default — a 7–30 day recovery window during which the name stays reserved and can't be reused. To purge it immediately (e.g. before recreating it via Terraform):

aws secretsmanager delete-secret \
  --secret-id first_national_bank/mongo_credentials \
  --force-delete-without-recovery

Skips the recovery grace period entirely — fine for a dev/learning secret like this one, not something to reach for on a secret protecting real production data.

5Teardown

terraform destroy

Without recovery_window_in_days = 0 set on the secret resource, destroying it only schedules deletion — re-running apply soon after will hit InvalidRequestException: already scheduled for deletion unless you force-delete it first, per step 4.
